## Abstract

The readiness potential (RP)—a key ERP correlate of upcoming action—is known to precede subjects' reports of their decision to move. Some view this as evidence against a causal role for consciousness in human decision-making and thus against free-will. But previous work focused on arbitrary decisions—purposeless, unreasoned, and without consequences. It remains unknown to what degree the RP generalizes to deliberate, more ecological decisions. We directly compared deliberate and arbitrary decision-making during a $1000-donation task to non-profit organizations. While we found the expected RPs for arbitrary decisions, they were strikingly absent for deliberate ones. Our results and drift-diffusion model are congruent with the RP representing accumulation of noisy, random fluctuations that drive arbitrary—but not deliberate—decisions. They further point to different neural mechanisms underlying deliberate and arbitrary decisions, challenging the generalizability of studies that argue for no causal role for consciousness in decision-making to real-life decisions.

**Editorial note:** This article has been through an editorial process in which the authors decide how to respond to the issues raised during peer review. The Reviewing Editor's assessment is that all the issues have been addressed ([see decision letter](/articles/39787/figures#SA1)).

## Introduction

Humans typically experience freely selecting between alternative courses of action, say, when ordering a particular item off a restaurant menu. Yet a series of human studies using electroencephalography (EEG) ([Haggard and Eimer, 1999](#bib23); [Libet et al., 1983](#bib40); [Salvaris and Haggard, 2014](#bib62)), fMRI ([Bode and Haynes, 2009](#bib3); [Bode et al., 2011](#bib2); [Soon et al., 2008](#bib73); [Soon et al., 2013](#bib74)), intracranial ([Perez et al., 2015](#bib55)), and single-cell recordings ([Fried et al., 2011](#bib16)) challenged the veridicality of this common experience. These studies found neural correlates of decision processes hundreds of milliseconds and even seconds prior to the moment that subjects reported having consciously decided.

The seminal research that launched this series of studies was conducted by Benjamin Libet and colleagues ([Libet et al., 1983](#bib40)). There, the authors showed that the readiness potential (RP)—a ramp-up in EEG negativity before movement onset, thought to originate from the presupplementary motor area (pre-SMA)—began before subjects reported a conscious decision to act. Libet and colleagues took the RP to be a marker for an unconscious decision to act ([Libet et al., 1983](#bib40); [Soon et al., 2008](#bib73)) that, once it begins, ballistically leads to action ([Shibasaki and Hallett, 2006](#bib69)). Under that interpretation, the fact that RP onset precedes the report of the onset of the conscious decision to act was taken as evidence that decisions about actions are made unconsciously. And thus the subjective human experience of freely and consciously deciding to act is but an illusion ([Harris, 2012](#bib26); [Libet et al., 1983](#bib40); [Wegner, 2002](#bib85)). # How the experiment that nearly killed free will is still haunting neuroscience

Neuroscience could hold the key to answering one of philosophy’s oldest questions

Bird flying out of cage shaped like human head.

Photo credit: Eiko Ojala

[Nate Scharping](/author/nate-scharping)

Published: March 18, 2026 at 6:00 pm

---

Whether or not we have free will is a question philosophers have been debating for millennia. In the early 1980s, there was a brief moment when it appeared the debate may finally have been settled.

The potential solution came not from philosophy, but neuroscience.

The answer, somewhat depressingly, was that free will didn’t exist. [Experiments carried out](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OjCt-L0Ph5o) by the neuroscientist Benjamin Libet appeared to show decisions being made in the [brain](https://www.sciencefocus.com/the-human-body/human-brain) before people were even aware of them.

It was as if science had finally revealed the strings of the puppet master controlling our thoughts and actions.

To even casual observers of the history of inquiries into free will, this pronouncement felt premature. Thankfully, they were right.

Scientists today are [much more sceptical](https://www.sciencefocus.com/the-human-body/free-will) not only of the idea that free will doesn’t exist, but also of the notion that brain scans will ever definitively prove or disprove its existence. But why?

## How you make a decision

Ultimately, the question of free will may be best left to philosophers, but that doesn’t mean it’s a topic neuroscientists should ignore.

Experiments into how the human brain makes decisions have led to important insights into neurology and psychology, and have expanded our understanding of the brain’s inner workings.

Those experiments include the ones Libet conducted in the 1980s, which, although viewed in a more critical light now, paved the way for decades of innovative research.

The [experiments were simple](https://academic.oup.com/brain/article-abstract/106/3/623/271932?redirectedFrom=fulltext&login=false). Libet attached volunteers to an electroencephalogram (EEG) machine to monitor their brain activity, then placed a button in front of them and asked them to decide when they wanted to press it.

While they were deciding, they had to watch a timer, consisting of a dot moving around the inside of a circle (like a second hand on a clock). Each volunteer had to note the dot’s position when they decided to press the button.

With the EEGs, Libet was looking for something called a [readiness potential](https://www.cell.com/trends/cognitive-sciences/fulltext/S1364-6613%2821%2900093-0), a build-up of activity in the brain’s motor cortex that precedes a muscle movement.

He was hoping to see how a volunteer’s awareness of their decision to move (their noting of the dot’s position) lined up with their readiness potential.

The distinct pattern of readiness potentials turned up in the volunteers’ EEGs around 200 milliseconds earlier than their decisions to press the button. In other words, their brains were preparing to press, before they were aware of having decided to press.

The interpretation was that “unconscious processes precede and determine our intentional actions,” says [Prof Marcel Brass](https://social-intelligence-group.github.io/team/), a cognitive neuroscientist at the Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin.

“In principle, people have taken that as evidence that we don’t have free will, or at least not conscious free will.”

![](https://c02.purpledshub.com/uploads/sites/41/2026/03/free-will-neuroscience-brain.jpg?webp=1&w=1200)

It comes down to the fact that all we are is biology, over which we have no control - Image credit: Alicia Blasco

It’s an existentially bracing finding, if true. But, as Brass notes, [subsequent researchers](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1053810021000970?via%3Dihub) have critiqued both Libet’s methodology and conclusions.

For example, the study relies on volunteers’ judgment of when they made a decision – hardly a sure thing. The experiment also looked at very simple, almost instinctual decisions. Would it hold for more complex decisions, like deciding whether to take a new job, or to get married?

Other scientists have argued that, while Libet found a signal of the brain preparing to act, those preparations [could still be overridden](https://www.jneurosci.org/content/27/34/9141?ijkey=7c18d50c0f545a930c5453c06a540284d7789b50&keytype2=tf%5Fipsecsha).

Indeed, later experiments suggested that it might be possible – people could countermand the actions indicated by the readiness potentials (although further experiments indicate there may not actually be enough time to do so).

Brass believes that what Libet saw wasn’t the brain beginning to carry out an action, but rather the brain formulating a decision about what to do.

“People accumulate evidence for a specific decision and then, when this hits a threshold, they make the decision,” he says. “That means the brain activity reflects the decision process, but it’s not deterministic.”

More recent work looking at what’s called [lateralised readiness potentials](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3953213/), which compare both hemispheres of the brain, bears this theory out.

When participants are asked to make a simple yes or no choice, [researchers see activity](https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822%2809%2901543-7?script=true) predicting both ‘yes’ and ‘no’, building on separate sides of the brain. When activity on one side crosses a threshold, the brain makes a choice.

Experiments like this have convinced Brass that neuroscience has yet to disprove the concept of free will. It’s also just common sense, he says.

“If there \[were a\] process in our brains that determines what we’re going to do, we would be extremely inflexible,” Brass says. “In principle, we must be able to redesign or change our course of action on a relatively short-term basis.”

* [It's time to change your relationship with dopamine](https://www.sciencefocus.com/science/dopamine-detox-focus-mood)
* [The simple ways you can change your personality, according to a cognitive neuroscientist](https://www.sciencefocus.com/wellbeing/how-to-change-your-personality-neuroscience)

## A counterpoint

Not everyone agrees that free will exists. Speaking on the [_BBC Science Focus_ podcast](https://www.sciencefocus.com/the-human-body/you-dont-have-free-will), [Prof Robert Sapolsky](https://profiles.stanford.edu/robert-sapolsky), a primatologist and neuroscientist from Stanford University, in the US, argues that our conscious experience of free will is an illusion created by our minds.

“It comes down to the fact that all we are is biology, over which we have no control, interacting with the environment, over which we have no control. There’s nothing else there,” he says.

![Illustration showing a person holding two other people back from grabbing a basketball floating above a pedestal](https://c02.purpledshub.com/uploads/sites/41/2026/03/free-will-neuroscience-basketball.jpg?webp=1&w=1200)

The science points towards the existence of a spectrum of free will - Image credit: Alicia Blasco

It’s an argument grounded in the determinism of physics, where actions follow clearly defined laws: molecules don’t decide whether to react or not; objects don’t decide whether to obey the law of [gravity](https://www.sciencefocus.com/space/gravity).

Based on my research, here is a comprehensive summary of the evidence and arguments on both sides of this debate.

---

## Free Will and Neuroscience: A Deeply Contested Debate

The conclusion that "free will is an illusion" based on neuroscience is **not settled science**—it is one position in an active, multi-decade controversy involving neuroscientists and philosophers. Below are the strongest studies and arguments from both sides.

---

### I. Evidence Cited by Those Who Say Free Will Is an Illusion

#### 1. Libet's Readiness Potential Experiments (1983)
**Study:** Benjamin Libet, Curt Riley Jr., Robert W. Gill, and Alan Knight, *Brain* **106**(3):623–642 (1983).

Libet attached EEG electrodes to participants' scalps and asked them to flex their wrist at a moment of their choosing while watching a clock-like timer. Participants reported the clock hand's position when they first became conscious of their *intention* to move. Libet found that a slow build-up of brain activity—the **readiness potential (RP)**—began on average **~550 ms before the movement** and **~350 ms before the reported conscious intention**. Libet concluded that "unconscious processes precede and determine our intentional actions."

#### 2. Soon, Haynes, and Colleagues' fMRI Studies (2008, 2013)
**Study 1:** Chun Siong Soon, Markus Brass, Hans-Christoph Heiss, John-Dylan Haynes, "Unconscious determinants of free decisions in the human brain," *Nature Neuroscience* **11**(5):543–545 (2008).

Using fMRI, the team decoded participants' upcoming choices (press left or right button) from activity in the prefrontal and parietal cortex **up to 7–10 seconds before** the participant reported making a conscious decision. Prediction accuracy was ~60%—above chance but imperfect. The authors argued this showed decisions are unconsciously determined well before awareness.

**Study 2:** Soon, Brass, Heinze, and Haynes, "Predicting free choices for abstract intentions," *PNAS* **110**(13):5283–5288 (2013).

This study extended the finding: brain activity could predict whether participants would choose to add or subtract numbers up to **7 seconds** before conscious awareness.

#### 3. Deterministic/Reductionist Philosophical Arguments
Philosophers and scientists such as **Sam Harris** (*The Illusion of Conscious Will*, 2012) and **Daniel Wegner** (*The Illusion of Conscious Will*, 2002) argue that because every mental event has a neural precursor, conscious will is epiphenomenal—an illusion generated by the brain after the fact. **Robert Sapolsky** (Stanford neuroscientist/primatologist) makes this case from a broader determinist perspective: if all behavior follows from biology and environment over which we have no control, there is literally "nothing else there" beyond causal chains.

---

### II. Evidence and Arguments Against the "Illusion" Conclusion

#### 1. Schurger's Accumulator Model (2012) — A Reinterpretation of the RP
**Study:** Aaron Schurger, Jacobo D. Sitt, Stanislas Dehaene, "An accumulator model for spontaneous neural activity prior to self-initiated movement," *PNAS* **109**(42):E2904–E2913 (2012).

This is arguably the most important counter-argument. Schurger showed that the RP does **not** reflect a deterministic "decision-making" process but rather **spontaneous neural noise**. His model demonstrates that if the brain uses a common decision machinery—a stochastic accumulator that drifts randomly until it crosses a threshold—then theRP will naturally appear as a ramping signal even *before* the subject has made any decision. The RP is simply the brain's decision apparatus waiting for random fluctuations to reach threshold, not evidence of an unconscious decision already having been made. As **Marcel Brass** (Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin) summarizes: "the brain activity reflects the decision process, but it's not deterministic."

#### 2. Maoz, Yaffe, Koch, and Mudrik — No RP for Deliberate Decisions (2019)
**Study:** Uri Maoz, Gideon Yaffe, Christof Koch, Liad Mudrik, "Neural precursors of decisions that matter—an ERP study of deliberate and arbitrary choice," *eLife* **8**:e39787 (2019).

This is a critical study directly challenging the generalizability of Libet-style findings. The researchers compared **arbitrary** choices (randomly deciding when to press a button) with **deliberate** choices (deciding how much of $1,000 to donate to nonprofit organizations). They found:
- **RP was present for arbitrary decisions**, replicating Libet's results.
- **RP was strikingly absent for deliberate decisions.**

The authors concluded that the RP represents "accumulation of noisy, random fluctuations that drive arbitrary—but not deliberate—decisions," and that findings from arbitrary-movement tasks should **not** be generalized to real-life, consequential decisions. This directly undermines the claim that neuroscience has shown conscious will plays no causal role in decision-making.

#### 3. Methodological Criticisms of Libet's Experiment
- **Timing accuracy:** The entire argument depends on participants' subjective reports of when they became aware of their intention. These reports have been widely criticized as unreliable. As noted in the review by Brass and Haggard, "the study relies on volunteers' judgment of when they made a decision—hardly a sure thing."
- **Artificial task:** Libet's experiment involved a trivial, purposeless motor act (flicking a wrist). Critics argue this does not test the kind of deliberative reasoning central to free will debates.
- **RP ≠ Decision:** The readiness potential may reflect motor *preparation*, not a decision itself. Activity in both hemispheres can build up for competing options; the choice occurs when one side crosses threshold.

#### 4. "Free Won't" — Conscious Veto Power
Libet himself later argued that while we may lack "free will" (the ability to initiate an action consciously), we retain **"free won't"**—the capacity to consciously veto an action once it has been unconsciously initiated. Libet allowed ~150 ms for this veto. However, subsequent research (e.g., **Haggard, 2008**; **Kathleen Ainsworth Clarke's analysis**) has contested even this: some studies find that the neural precursor to *inhibition* also precedes conscious awareness of the decision to stop, suggesting the veto itself may not be freely chosen.

#### 5. The "Free Won't" Critique from Haggard and Others
**Haggard's review:** Patrick Haggard, "Human Volition: Towards a Neuroscience of Will," *Nature Reviews Neuroscience* **9**(12):934–946 (2008).

Haggard argues that volition is better understood as a multi-stage process involving intention formation, action selection, and monitoring—none of which maps cleanly onto Libet's binary "decided vs. didn't decide" framework. He emphasizes that conscious will may play a causal role in **sustaining** intentions and guiding attention toward goals, not merely in initiating discrete motor acts.

#### 6. Philosophical Objections
- **Category mistake:** Critics argue that asking "when does the brain decide?" assumes decisions are point-like neural events, when they may be distributed processes that cannot be pinned to a single moment.
- **Definition of free will:** The debate often conflates *libertarian* free will (the ability to have done otherwise in exactly the same circumstances) with *compatibilist* free will (acting according to one's own reasons, desires, and values without external coercion). Neuroscience may challenge the former but is largely irrelevant to the latter.
- **Harris and Wegner's arguments** are philosophical interpretations of empirical data, not empirical findings themselves—and their readings of the data are contested by many neuroscientists.

---

### III. Summary: What Is Actually Contested?

| Question | Pro-Illusion Position | Anti-Illusion / Contested Position |
|---|---|---|
| **Does RP indicate a decision?** | Yes—the brain decides before we know it. | No—RP is spontaneous noise (Schurger et al., 2012). |
| **Do fMRI predictions disprove free will?** | They show unconscious determination of choice. | Predictions are ~60% accurate at best; imperfect prediction ≠ no freedom. |
| **Are Libet findings generalizable?** | Yes—they reveal a fundamental feature of volition. | No—only apply to arbitrary, trivial choices (Maoz et al., 2019). |
| **Does conscious will have causal power?** | No—it is epiphenomenal. | Possibly via "free won't," sustained intention, and deliberative processes. |
| **Is the debate scientifically resolvable?** | Neuroscience has spoken. | The question may be philosophical rather than empirical; definitions matter enormously. |

### Bottom Line

The conclusion that free will is an illusion based on neuroscience is **highly contested**, even among scientists who work in this area. The strongest evidence against free will (Libet 1983; Soon et al. 2008/2013) has been challenged by equally rigorous studies showing that neural precursors of action differ fundamentally between arbitrary and deliberate decisions (Schurger et al. 2012; Maoz et al. 2019), and that the RP may reflect stochastic noise rather than a pre-decided outcome. Many neuroscientists—including **Patrick Haggard**, **Marcel Brass**, and **Kathleen Ainsworth Clarke**—have argued that Libet-style experiments tell us about the neuroscience of *arbitrary motor initiation*, not about conscious will in deliberative decision-making, and that the leap from "unconscious neural precursors exist" to "free will is an illusion" is not justified by the data.

The debate remains open at both the scientific and philosophical levels.
